title: Chapter 206 – The Furnace at Terrace Three
html:
[Terrace Three – Mo Yan]

Mo Yan has a voice now, and she does not know what to do with it.

It sits in her throat like a pebble she has swallowed by mistake. It is not painful. It is only there, a small hard thing at the base of the tongue, ready to come out if she opens her mouth, and she has spent four days not opening it. She eats with her mouth shut. She sleeps with her mouth shut. When Hua asks if she is tired, she nods, and when Jian asks if she wants to turn back, she shakes her head. She is eight years old and has been silent for six hundred and ten, and the habit is stronger than the wish to break it.

What would I even say?

She asks herself this, on the black water, in the bow of the boat, with her knees under her chin and the lantern throwing its small gold ring on the surface. She asks it again. The only answer is the dark.

Behind her the Ferryman poles on. His strokes are slower than they were. Each push of the long wood against nothing takes longer to begin and longer to end, and between the strokes he breathes, a dry thin rasp like a stick drawn across a fence. Mo Yan can hear it. She has always heard such things. It is the price of having no voice of your own: the ears learn to do twice the work.

He is dying, she thinks.

She does not say it. She turns, instead, and looks at him. He sits in the stern with his hood fallen back and the gray fabric of his cloak soaked black with lake-spray. His face is turned to the front. It is a long, narrow, lined face, as hollow as the face of an old horse, and in the lantern light she sees that it has begun to go clear at the edges, like breath on a window.

Their eyes meet.

He gives her a very small nod. It is the nod of an old man to a child who has noticed a thing and been kind enough not to mention it. Then he turns his gaze back to the dark and poles, once, twice, and the boat slides on.

* * *

The third landing is a fire.

She smells it long before she sees it: hot iron, charcoal, scorched oil, a breath of sulfur. The air thickens. The black water grows warm against the hull, then hot, and a pale vapor curls off it like steam from a kettle. The lantern light goes red. And then the darkness opens, as a hand opens, and there is a quay of dark red stone and a glow behind it that fills the whole of the sky.

"Hold on," says Jian, behind her. "It is going to be bright."

It is. It is the brightest thing she has ever seen. A mountain stands at the end of the quay, or something that was a mountain, a huge black cone with its top sliced away, and in the open crater a lake of molten light churns and glows. Chains hang down its sides. Great iron troughs run from the crater to the quay, filled with something white-gold and slow. Hundreds of shapes move along them, tiny with distance, bent over hammers and tongs.

The Terrace of Fire.

Mo Yan stands up in the boat without being asked. She puts one hand on the gunwale and leans out, wide-eyed, and the hot wind blows her braid straight back from her head. Somewhere in her chest the pebble in her throat gives a small hard shiver.

They are making something, she thinks.

They are. She can hear it. A deep slow rhythm under the roar, like a heart: clang, clang, clang, a hundred hammers in time. And under it, fainter, a tune. Someone is singing as they work. It is a low plain song with no words. It sounds like a thing that has been sung every day for six centuries and has worn smooth as a river stone.

Hua catches her by the back of the gown. "Careful, little one."

"Hot," Mo Yan thinks, and nearly says it aloud.

* * *

The Keeper of the Third Terrace is a woman called Dahl, and she is as wide as she is tall.

She waits on the quay with her arms folded, in a leather apron burned black at the hem, and a pair of thick-glassed goggles pushed up into a mass of iron-gray hair. Her forearms are the size of Mo Yan's legs. Her face is red with heat and creased with laughter lines, though she is not laughing now. She watches the boat come in as a farmer watches a stranger's cow come through the gate.

"Ferryman," she says.

"Keeper."

"You are late." Her voice is deep and gruff. "I banked the furnace an hour ago. Another hour and it would have gone out. Do you know what that costs?"

"I do."

"Then why are you late?"

"I carried passengers." The old man's voice is a thread. "Four. The first in six hundred years."

Dahl's eyes flick to the four. They move over Jian, with his staff and trembling hands, and Hua, with her bandage, and settle, at last, on the small bronze creature on Jian's shoulder, and then on Mo Yan.

"Hm," she says.

It is not a warm sound.

"We seek passage to the Fourth," says Jian. He steps onto the quay with care. "We are not enemies. We do not wish to disturb your work."

"Passage." The Keeper makes a noise like a bellows. "That is a joke. You think you can walk up my stair and ask the way like a peddler?"

"I think I can ask politely."

"You can. You will not get it." She uncrosses her arms. "A party came through two days ago. Seven in gray silk. Their leader had a lantern and a cold, polite way of speaking. He asked for the furnace-key. I told him no. He said he would wait."

"Elder Ye."

"I did not catch his name. I did not care." Dahl bares her teeth. "He is in my guest house now, drinking my tea. He has been there two days. He says he is willing to be patient." She jerks her chin at Mo Yan. "He asked about the girl."

Hua stiffens. "What girl?"

"That one." Dahl's gaze does not leave Mo Yan's face. "He said she was a kind of key. That a child who could hear the Terraces would be a great help to the road. He said if she came to me, I should hold her."

The hot wind seems to stop.

Mo Yan feels the pebble in her throat go cold. She presses herself against Hua's leg. Hua's hand closes on her shoulder, hard enough to hurt, and does not let go.

"And?" says Jian. His voice is very quiet.

"And I said that I keep a furnace, not a prison." Dahl's mouth twists. "He smiled. He said that was a pity."

* * *

Dahl does not offer passage for nothing, and she says so in the first minute.

"Work," she says. She plants a hand like a ham on the edge of her anvil. "Everyone who crosses my Terrace works. The Founders' rule. A man who will not feed the fire has no business walking past it."

"I am an artifact refiner," says Jian.

"Are you."

"Rank four. Normal." He says it without pride. "Golden Core. I can work at my own rank, and perhaps a hair above."

"Hm." The Keeper looks him up and down. His trembling hands, his staff, the silver line along his jaw. "Your hands shake."

"Yes."

"A refiner with shaking hands is a danger to himself and his betters."

"I have worked with worse."

She grunts. Then she jerks her head toward the mountain. "Come."

The forge is the size of a courtyard. It sits at the foot of the crater on a platform of black glass, and the heat in it is a living thing, a pressure against the skin. Dozens of smiths work in it, men and women alike, bare-armed in leather, their faces glistening. None looks up. The great troughs of white-gold metal flow past, and the hammers fall, and a boy of ten stands on an upturned bucket to pump a bellows twice his size.

Dahl leads Jian to a tall iron frame at the back. In it hangs a thing like a giant's ladle, bent and scorched, with a hairline crack running down its throat.

"The blast-spout," she says. "It feeds the furnace its air. It cracked in the last quake. I can weld it, but a weld will not hold. The metal is Founders' alloy. It will not take a seam." Her jaw tightens. "I have waited forty years for someone who could mend it."

Jian walks around the frame. He puts out a shaking hand and lays his palm on the cracked iron. The heat sears. He does not flinch.

Mo Yan watches his face. His eyes go still and a little unfocused, the way they do when he reads what no one else can see, and under her feet the black glass floor gives a faint answering hum. She has heard that hum before. It comes from the place in him that is not quite him. For a moment the whole cracked iron seems to lean toward his hand, and she knows, as clearly as if he had spoken, that he is seeing the grain.

"I can mend it," he says slowly. "But not with a weld. The Founders built it to bend one way, and the quake bent it another."

"Then how?"

"With a pattern." He draws a breath. "If I realign the grain, the crack will close of its own accord. It will take time. And it will take..." He glances at his hands. "A steady touch."

"You have not got one."

"No."

"Then why do you stand there?"

"Because I know a way to borrow one."

He turns his head. Mo Yan has crept up behind him, small and silent in her patched gown, with her eyes huge. She is watching the cracked iron. She is watching it with a look he has seen before, on Hua's face, in the Roll Room: the look of someone who can feel a thing that others cannot.

"Mo Yan," he says. "Will you help me?"

She nods.

"I will do the work. You will hold the pattern. I will tell you where, and you will tell the iron to stay." He kneels, carefully, in front of her. "It will not hurt. But it will tire you."

She lays her small palm over his shaking one.

It takes four hours. The smiths stop to watch, one by one, and Dahl stands with her arms folded and her face like a rock. Jian works with the hammer and a pair of copper tongs, tapping the iron in a slow rhythm, and Mo Yan's hand steadies his wrist with a small cool pressure. The grain moves. The crack narrows. At the end of the fourth hour, the hairline vanishes as if it had never been, and the blast-spout rings under the last tap with a note as clear as a struck glass.

Mo Yan has never held a pattern before, and it is stranger than she expected.

It is like holding a long thin thread that is also a river. The iron is hot, and the heat goes up her arm, but under the heat she feels the metal's wanting: a slow stubborn lean toward the way it was made. Jian's hand taps. She holds. The grain turns, a hair at a time, and her small fingers cramp and ache and do not let go. At the end of the second hour she can no longer feel her wrist. At the end of the third she is singing under her breath, without sound, the Ferryman's old tune, to keep the thread from slipping.

When it is done, she sits down on the black glass floor and laughs. Nobody hears it. It is only breath. But the smiths, one by one, turn to look at the small girl in the patched gown with her braid undone, grinning at nothing, and a woman with a ruined hand reaches out and gently pats her head.

Dahl says nothing. She walks to the frame, runs a thick thumb down the length of the mended throat, and stops.

"Forty years," she says.

"I am sorry it took so long."

"It is not you who took it." She turns, and for the first time her broad red face breaks into something like a smile. "Passage granted. And a bed, and supper. And you may tell that silk-gowned gentleman in my guest house that the Keeper of the Third Terrace would be obliged if he stayed there."

They are put in a different guest house, at the far end of the quay, with a door that locks from inside.

It is a low stone building built against the cooling flank of the mountain, with a roof of black slate and a window that looks out on the churning light. There is a stove, a table, three narrow beds. The air is dry and hot. Hua puts the bar across the door, and Jian sits on the edge of a bed with his staff across his lap, and Mo Yan sits cross-legged in the middle of the floor and stares at the fire.

He wants me, she thinks.

She has known it since Terrace Two. She has felt it, a thin cold thread at the edge of her hearing, like a finger moving over a glass rim. It is not a sound. It is the shape of attention. Someone is listening to her listen. It is the same pressure she felt in the Dock, the same patient pull as the Door Seven, except this one is thinner, sharper, and it has a hook in it.

"Mo Yan," says Hua.

She looks up.

Her mother kneels in front of her, and takes both her hands in her own, and the bandaged one is rough and warm. Hua's face is steady. Her eyes are gray and dark and far too bright.

"I am going to say something," she says. "And you do not have to answer. You do not have to do anything. Only listen."

Mo Yan nods.

"I do not remember you being born." Hua's voice is low and clear. "I do not remember your first word, or your first step, or the sound of your laugh. I have been told that you were very small and very quiet and that you loved to be carried. I believe it. I do not remember." She swallows. "But I know, in my bones, that I would not give you to that man for a thousand roads. Not for the Ninth Terrace. Not for the Stair-Father. Not for anything in this world or any other."

Mo Yan's eyes sting.

"If you want to go home, we go home. Tonight. If you want to stay and be brave, I will stay with you, and I will hold you every night." Hua's thumb moves over the back of her hand. "But you do not have to be a key. You never did. You are a girl."

Mo Yan sits very still.

The pebble in her throat is hot now. It burns. She opens her mouth, and shuts it. She opens it again.

"Mama," she says.

It is the smallest sound in the world. It is hoarse and cracked and barely a breath. But it hangs in the hot dry air of the guest house like a bell, and she sees her mother's face change.

"Say it again," whispers Hua.

"Mama."

Hua makes a sound that is half sob and half laugh. She pulls the girl into her arms, hard, so hard her ribs creak, and Mo Yan clings to her with both fists in her gown. The world is a blur of hot light and tears. She hears Jian get up from the bed and go to the window, with his back to them, and stand there with his shoulders very straight.

"Mama," she says again, into the rough wool. Her voice is a crow's voice. It is the most beautiful thing she has ever heard.

* * *

The Ferryman comes to the guest house at midnight, alone, and does not come in.

She hears him at the door. A scrape of boot, a hesitation, a knock so soft she nearly takes it for a log settling in the stove. Hua is asleep in the next bed. Jian sits by the window in the dark, awake, watching the glow of the crater, and he rises without a word and draws the bar.

The old man stands on the step with his hood down.

In the red light of the mountain, he looks like a figure cut from smoke. He has thinned. Mo Yan can see the planks of the quay through his legs. His eyes are two coins, dull and bright by turns, and his hands, at his sides, are shaking.

"Ferryman," says Jian.

"Forgive me." The dry voice is almost a whisper. "I did not wish to wake the child."

"She is awake."

Mo Yan has crept to the door. She stands behind Jian's elbow in her nightgown, with bare feet on the hot stone. The Ferryman turns his hood toward her. A tired, kind, ghost-gray smile crosses his face.

"I have a gift," he says. "For the little one."

He holds out his hand. In it lies a small thing, no larger than a thumb. It is a bell. It is made of black glass, and it has no clapper, and on its rim someone has etched a tiny ship with a single sail.

"It was the first fare," he says. "A girl gave it to me in the first week. She was nine. She had no coin, no lifespan to spare, only a toy her father had made. I said I could not take it. She said she would not cross unless I did." A dry rustle. "I have kept it six hundred years. I thought: one day, someone will ask for the road, and I will have a thing to give them in return."

Mo Yan takes the bell. It is cool and smooth and surprisingly heavy.

"It rings," says the Ferryman, "when someone on the water is lost. The sound is very small. But you will hear it. You hear everything."

"Thank you," says Mo Yan.

It comes out of her easily this time, like a word she has said a hundred times. The Ferryman's face changes. For an instant the gray, hollow, ghostlike features are young, and astonished, and glad.

"There," he says. "There it is."

"Ferryman—" says Jian.

"I am not finished." The old man lifts a hand. "I have one more crossing in me. One. The boat can carry us to the Fourth Landing, and the fare will be paid. After that I do not think the keel will hold." His voice cracks. "I would like it to be a good one."

"You are dying."

"I am loose from the keel." The Ferryman's smile is gentle. "It is not the same. I was a man once, and then I was a road. And now the road wants a new boatman." He looks past Jian, at the far dark of the quay. "I wanted you to know I do not blame you for not taking the seat. It is a lonely thing, and I would not wish it on any of the children."

"Someone will have to."

"Yes. Not you." His eyes fall on Mo Yan. "Not her. Someone who has already been alone."

He bows. It is a deep, stiff, old-fashioned bow, with his bony hand pressed to his heart, and the red light shines through him like a lantern through paper.

"Sleep," he says. "I will wake you at dawn."

* * *

The last crossing is the quietest of all.

She sits in the bow with the black glass bell in her fist. Jian and Hua sit behind her. Pebble is a warm lump in her lap, rattling softly, refusing to look at the water. The boat slides across the dark without a sound, and the glow of the mountain falls behind them, and for a long time there is nothing but black and the faint ring of the lantern.

The Ferryman poles. His strokes are very slow now. Between them he sings.

She did not hear it begin. It is a low, breathy, old man's voice, thin as thread, and the tune is the same as the song of the forge. It wanders. It forgets its words. It comes back. She leans her head against Hua's knee and listens, and finds that she knows it. Not from the mountain. From before. From a bed, in the dark, with a ring of lamps overhead, and a warm hand tucking a blanket round her chin.

Hush, the hand had said. Hush, little one. The boat will take you home.

She looks up. The Ferryman's hood has fallen back. His face is turned to the dark, and the clear, shining edge of him has crept inward until there is almost nothing left but the shape of a man and the sound.

"Ferryman," she says.

"Yes, child?"

"You sang to us."

"I did." There is a smile in the dry voice. "In the beds. Every night. For a hundred years. It seemed little enough to do."

"Thank you."

"You have said that."

"I want to keep saying it."

He laughs. It is a small, bright, cracked sound, and the lantern flame trembles. "Then say it at the other end, little one," he says. "I shall be listening."

The boat touches the quay.

It does not bump. It does not rock. It simply stops, as a held breath stops, and the long black pole slides from the Ferryman's hands and lies across the thwarts. The old man sits where he is. His head is bowed. His gray cloak lies in folds on the bench. Under it, there is nothing at all.

Mo Yan stares at the empty cloak.

Behind her Hua draws a long, shaking breath. Jian does not speak. Overhead, in the dark, one by one, the lamps along the Fourth Landing's quay are going out. They have waited six hundred years for a boatman, and they have understood, as lamps do, that he is not coming back. Not suddenly. Not in a rush. They dim, and flicker, and fade, like candles at the end of a long vigil, until at last the only light is the one in the bow of the boat, small and gold and steady.

She opens her fist. The little black bell lies on her palm. She holds it up. Very gently, she shakes it.

It rings.

It is the smallest sound she has ever heard. A single clear note, thin and silver, that goes out over the dark water and does not come back. But it carries. It carries all the way to the end of the world, through the dark and the cold and the sleeping weight of the lake, and far across the lake, from somewhere deep under the keel, a vast slow voice answers.

Hello, says the one under the lake. Hello, little one. I remember the beds. I remember every one of you. I was so very sorry, and I did not know how to say it.

And then, very softly, so softly that she is not sure she has not imagined it, in a voice she has heard in no dream:

Thank you for the song.
